content:
I hadn't previously known about @Cody Roux's name-the-biggest-number Rocq project, but after @Marc Huisinga mentioned it to me I thought we should have it, too.

Bonus points, I think for not jumping too far ahead: don't just try to win, try to do "the next bigger number" after the current "biggest number". That will make it more fun for everyone.

https://github.com/kim-em/name-the-biggest-number is open for PRs. If you follow the rules, your PRs get merged automatically. (The rule enforcement isn't bullet-proof, play nice.)

Awesome! I am very sad I didn't beat the current contender in the Rocq version, it was hard work but would have been feasible.

One reason I didn't really push it in Lean was the classical/intuitionistic distinction, which should qualitatively change the game a bit (e.g. Busy Beaver should come into play quite early now).

That being said it should be fun in Lean! And might give incentive to flesh out computability theory a bit.
One should clarify the rules on constructivity. The repo has @Cody Roux’s original constructivity requirement, but you also allow mathlib.

Is this going to cap out at
"the output of a largest function defined in a strongly normalising calculus with proof theoretic strength of ZFC + finitely many inaccessibles"?

Right. I see 2 easy choices:

  1. require the definition to be computable, but all proofs in the definition and that it is the contender may be classical.
  2. No restrictions on definition or proof (except axioms of course)

More subtle rules could ask that the number be recursive, e.g. or exclude classical axioms (I think that's a bad idea)

Jeremy Chen said:

Is this going to cap out at
"the output of a largest function defined in a strongly normalising calculus with proof theoretic strength of ZFC + finitely many inaccessibles"?

Yes, or a little before. But it's more work than one would expect with an English hand wavy proof.

Indeed proving that that number is larger than the previous ones should be a nice exercise in meta-programing.
definitely a big number. probably bigger than 1 million.

Cody Roux said:

Indeed proving that that number is larger than the previous ones should be a nice exercise in meta-programing.

So this would be, getting <previous contender>, taking its kernel term, determining the maximum universe level it uses, then embed it into your calculus. Definitely a challenge to get in under a minute :)

Yes, basically formalizing Lean with k universes without axioms, and type checking the term.

Not trivial.
I made a PR adding a "small" version of Graham's number (so its still beatable), but some workflow appears to be stuck
@Felix Pernegger, for now I need to approve CI for new contributors. But how about we don't jump ahead? Even G_1 is too big to merely beat 42.

Interesting game! I wonder if it would be a good idea to require small numbers (e.g. below 10↑↑3 in Knuth's notation) to have some sort of special property for submission, in order to avoid submissions consisting of only a long decimal expansion in the meantime. (For example maybe Belphegor's prime would be a notable enough property for a submission?)
